title: The rich fool (Luke 12:16–21)
hookLine: a man plans bigger barns for his surplus and dies that night

cards: It starts with a family fight. Someone in the crowd shouts at Jesus: tell my brother to split the inheritance with me. Jesus won't referee.
He tells a story instead. A rich man's land has a bumper year, more grain than his barns can hold. He lies awake, talking it over with himself.
What shall I do? I know: I'll tear down my barns and build bigger ones. I'll store everything.
Then I'll say to my soul: you're set for years. Eat, drink, enjoy. It's a good plan.

teach.b: Hear him: my crops, my barns, my fruits, my goods, my soul. I, my and mine, again and again. Nobody else is in the plan: no family, no workers, no neighbor.

He even talks to his own soul, as if it's the only one in the room. The old King James Bible gives his words: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry."
And the answer: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?"

teach.h: NOT A THIEF. NOT A CHEAT.
teach.b: He isn't a thief or a cheat; the land just produced. Saving isn't the problem either: the Bible praises the ant for storing food. His mistake is quieter.

teach.h: HE THINKS THE BARN IS HIS LIFE.
teach.b: He thinks the barn is his life.
Jesus says it plainly just before the story: a man's life doesn't consist in the abundance of the things he owns. And fool here doesn't mean stupid; he's clearly clever.
In the Bible a fool is someone who lives as if God weren't there. Whose? He's about to leave it all to someone else, which is exactly what the brother in the crowd was fighting over.
Luke ends with one more line: so is anyone who stores up treasure for himself and isn't rich toward God. Christians have heard rich toward God as generosity, prayer, a life turned outward.
Luke's answer, a few verses on, is simple: give.

how: Many Christians read this parable as a warning against greed and a call to generosity, and it's often preached alongside giving to the poor, tithing, or simplifying how they live.

o: someone short on brains or common sense
a jester who entertains a king's court
someone who lives as if God weren't there

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: tell my brother to split it

s: the rich man got his wealth by cheating
the text says his ground brought forth plentifully. he didn't steal anything. his mistake was thinking the barn was his life.
the story begins with a family fight over money
someone asks Jesus to make his brother split the inheritance. Jesus answers with this story.
he's clever enough. in the Bible a fool lives as if God weren't there.

games.q: you're the rich man. the harvest is bigger than your barns. what do you decide?
o: share the extra with the village.
tear down my barns, build bigger ones, and take it easy for years.
sell it all and give the money to the poor.
games.why: he builds bigger barns and tells his soul to eat, drink and be merry. that night God calls him a fool: "then whose shall those things be?"

practice: Walk through your home in your mind: the closet, the drawer you never open. Find one thing you keep just to keep it, like a coat you never wear, and picture who could use it.
If you pray, ask where it should go; if not, just picture it leaving your barn and landing where it's needed.

wordCard.voice: Fool. Not stupid, in the Bible's sense, but someone who lives as if God weren't there, like the man building bigger barns for a life only he controlled.

orig.note: Greek: fool. literally "without mind," someone who doesn't think things through.

carryVoice: Your line: you can't take the barn. But you can be rich toward God. Thirty days now, a whole month.
